AGRICULTURE (SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) Yes Sir. 
The first ever National Agriculture Policy was announced by 
Government on 28th July, 2000. 
(b) The National Agriculture Policy states that Government will 
endeavour to create a favourable economic environment for 
increasing capital formation and fa rmer's own investments by removal 
of distortions in the incentive regime for agriculture, improving the 
terms of trade with manufacturing sectors and bringing about external 
and domestic market reforms, backed by rationalization of domestic 
tax structure. Commodity-wise strategies and arrangements for 
protecting the grower from adverse impact of undue price fluctuations 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [22 February, 2001] 
in the world markets and for promot ing exports will be formulated. A 
favourable economic environment and supportive public management 
system will be created for promotion of agricultural exports. Import 
duties on manufactured commodities used in agriculture will be 
rationalized and appropriate tariffs protection will be provided. The 
domestic agricultural market will be liberalized and all controls and 
regulations hindering increase in farmers' income will be reviewed 
and abolished to ensure that agriculturists receive prices 
commensurate with their efforts. 
Public investment for narrowing regional imbalances, accelerating 
development of supportive infrastructure for agriculture and rural 
development particularly rural conn ectivity will be stepped up. Input 
subsidy reforms will be pursued as a combination of price and 
institutional reforms to cut down cost of these inputs for agriculture. 
Resource allocation regime will be reviewed with a view to 
rechannelizing the available resources from support measures towards 
asset formation in rural sector. 
Private sector investment in agriculture will also be encouraged 
more particularly in areas like agricultural re search, human, resource 
development, post-harvest management and marketing with a view to 
reducing  post-harvest losses and ensuring a  better return to the 
grower. 
National Agriculture Insurance Scheme covering all farmers and 
all crops throughout the country, with built in provisions for 
insulating farmers from financial distress caused by natural disasters 
and making agriculture financially viable, will be made more farmer- 
specific and effective. Endeavour w ill be made to provide a package 
insurance policy for the farmers, ri ght from sowing of the crops to 
post-harvest operations, including market fluctuations in the prices of 
agricultural produce.

RESOLUTION 
In order to reduce storage and transit losses of foodgrains at 
farm and commercial level, to modernise the system of handling, 
storage and transportation of the foodgrains procured by the Food 
Corporation of India (FCI) and to bring in additionality of resources 
through private sector involvement, the Government has approved a 
National Policy on Handling, Storage and Transportation of 
Foodgrains, details of which are given below:—  
1. Objectives of the Policy 
The main objectives of the policy are: 
i. to reduce storage and transit losses at farm level where 
about 70% of the total foodgrain production is retained 
and consumed and also to encourage the farmers to 
adopt scientific storage methods. 
ii. to modernise the system of handling, storage and 
transportation of the foodgrains procured by the Food 
Corporation of India (FCI). 
iii. to harness efforts and resources of public and private 
106 

{22 February, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
sectors, both domestic and ' foreign to build and 
operate infrastructure for introduction of bulk 
handling, storage and transportation of foodgrains in 
the country. 
2. Policy for house-hold siorage 
2.1 Since the house-hold sector retains about 70% of the 
total production and substantial quantities of foodgrains 
are wasted due to improper storage at farm level, the 
major focus is on the improvement of storage standards 
at farm level. Presently, the only scheme targeting this 
need is the Save Grain Campaign, which popularises the 
use of metallic and non-metallic storage structures and 
educates the farmers about the adoption of scientific 
storage methods. The scheme also aims at development/ 
improvement of non-metallic traditional storage structures. 
2.2 In order to have a greater success in this area, following 
initiatives have been approved:— 
(i) introduction of a scheme to encourage use of metal 
bins as well as non-metall ic storage structures at 
individual farm level and construction of KCC bins at 
community level with appropriate financial incentives. 
(ii) strengthening of the existing research and training 
components of the Save Grain Campaign Scheme for 
scientific storage and preservation of foodgrains and 
their propagation among farmers. 
3. Modernisation    and    Upgradation    of   Bulk    Grain    Handling 
Infrastructure 
3.1 In order to reduce storage losses, it is necessary to 
develop and modernise the infrastructure for integrated 
bulk handling storage and transportation in India. The 
thrust of the policy should be:—  
(i) encouragement or mechani cal harvesting, cleaning and 
drying at farm and mandi level. 
107 

RAJYA SABHA [22 February, 2001] 
(ii) transportation of grains from farm to silos by specially 
designed trucks. 
(iii) construction of a chain of silos at procurement as well as 
distribution points. 
(iv) transportation of grain from silos to railhead and 
thereafter to pre-determined destinations by specially 
designed trucks/rail wagons (with top filling and bottom 
discharge mechanism)/dedicated trains. 
(v) declaration of foodgrains storage as infrastructure. 
3.2 For storage of foodgrains procured by the FCI, integrated 
bulk handling facilities with silos of large capacity for wheat 
along with testing facilities for quality control would be 
created at about 20 identified central locations  in producing 
and consuming areas as well as a few port towns. These 
facilities, including the infrastru cture for bulk transportation 
to these centres, will be created and maintained in the 
private sector under the overa ll co-ordination of the FCI. 
The design of special top fitting and bottom discharge 
wagons would be decided in consultation with the Ministry of 
Railways. The Ministry of Railways will also be consulted 
while deciding the locations and the circuits where these 
wagons would ply. FCI will guarantee utilisation of these 
facilities to the extent of 100% for the first ten years and 
75% for the next ten years. From these points, secondary 
transportation of foodgrains would be made in bag form to 
about 500 godowns in important central locations in different 
States to be owned and maintained by the FCI. Further 
transportation to the consuming centres for retail distribution 
under the Public Distribution System will be carried out by 
the State Governments. 
3.3 The private sector will be encouraged to build storage 
capacities in which they will store and maintain foodgrains 
procured by the Government agencies, for which they will be 
entitled to storage charges. 
108 

[22 February, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
3.4 The private sector participation should be sought and 
encouraged for development of infrastructure for the 
integrated bulk handling, storage and transportation 
through—  
(i) measures such as Build-Own-Operate-Transfer (BOOT), 
Build-Own-Lease-Transfer (BOLT), Build-Own-Opcrate 
(BOO), Lease-Develop-Operat e (LDO), Joint Ventures 
etc. 
(ii) generation of funds through  public issues by  private 
enterprises 
(iii) automatic approval for Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) 
upto 100% 
(iv) loans  from   financial  institutions,  NABARD,  external 
commercial borrowings 
(v) fiscal incentives as given below: 
(a) 100% deduction in profit for the purpose of Income 
Tax for the first five years and 30% deduction in profit 
for the next five years. 
(b) deduction of 40% of the profits derived by financial 
institutions financing such projects, as provided to 
financial corporations engaged, inter-alia, in providing 
long term finance for agricultural development. 
(c) customs duty exemption for items not manufactured in 
India, on a case-to-case basis, subject to a list of such 
equipment being submitted in advance. 
4. Development of Infrastructure Facilities at Ports 
India has been traditionally the importer of foodgrains and, 
therefore the infrastructure facilities available at the ports arc 
basically meant for unloading operations and not for exports. For 
unloading operations ship gears are normally used. Even the latest 
mechanised facilities at Jawaharlal  Nehru Port, Navi Mumbai have 
been designed for import purposes only. There is also lack of general 
109 

RAJYA SABHA [22 February, 2001] 
cargo berths at the major ports and very limited warehousing facilities 
are available for the storage of f oodgrains at ports. For creating the 
proper port facilities for foodgrains meant for export in due course, 
the infrastructure facilities would have to be developed for which 
following actions are required: 
(i) identification of ports to be developed for purposes of 
export of foodgrains. The distribution of foodgrains 
traffic may spread over to the non-traditional ports which 
have spare capacity like New Mangalore and Cochin 
ports; 
(ii) development of more general cargo berths at the ports 
through ports' own investment/private participation; 
(iii) water front/berths can be leased to the users who may be 
encouraged to put up their own facilities; and 
(iv) development of dedicated modern foodgrains handling 
facilities at selected ports. 
5. Role of the Central Government 
The Central Government would: 
(a) facilitate    speedy    clearance    of    projects    concerning 
development of infrastructure for bulk handling 
transportation and storage of foodgrains by setting up an 
Approval Board competent to take final decision; 
(b) enter into bilateral agreements with other countries/ 
international agencies for providing technical/financial 
assistance; 
(c) take necessary legislative/administrative measures for 
removing impediments with regard to stock control 
Orders/movement control Orders framed by various 
State Governments; 
(d) utilize the services of an existing independent regulatory 
mechanism for fixing/regulating tariff for various 
operations, such as cleaning, drying, storage, 
transportation, etc.; 
110 

[22 February, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) make available facilities of the Railways for bulk 
transportation; 
(f) promote negotiable Warehouse Receipt System by which 
farmers could hold their grains back from market and 
meet their working capita l/short term requirement by 
borrowing from Banks against these receipts; and 
(g) promote research for development of alternate storage 
technologies like Vacuum Process Storage (VPS) 
technology which would ensu re longer shelf life of 
foodgrains  and   help  export  of foodgrains in  vacuum 
packs. 
6. Role of the State Government 
The State Government would help in : 
(a) acquisition of land required for various projects as for  
public purpose; and 
(b) making available other facilities such as water, power, 
road, etc.

quotes from the audit review on Public Distribution System included 
in the Comptroller and Auditor General of India's Report No. 3 of 
2000 laid on the Table of the Parliament during the Winter Session. 
(b) Public Distribution System is implemented under the joint 
responsibility of the Central and State Governments/UT 
Administrations. The Central Government is responsible for 
procurement, storage and transportation of the PDS commodities up 
to the designated Central godowns and making them available to the

portion of subsidised foodgrains to the open market Instances of

report on assessment of extent of diversion of foodgrains, sugar and 
edible oil from PDS in the country by the Tata Economic

the State Governments and UT Administrations concerned for taking 
remedial steps. 
(f) The major causes of diversi on cited in the TECS study are 
bulk diversion from godowns, bogus units in ration cards, 
underweighment at various levels, illiteracy of consumers, low profit 
margins for Fair Price Shops (FPS) owners, floating populations, 
fictitious distribution agencies, non-availability/irregular supply and 
inferiors quality with foreign particles. The State Governments have 
been requested to closely monitor the PDS at the Fair Price Shop 
(FPS) and other levels and to make arrangement for distribution of 
PDS commodities in a transparent and accountable manner by 
involvement of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs). Involvement of 
Panchayati Raj Institution in the implementation of TPDS as a 
measure of social audit wilt make the system more transparent and 
accountable and thereby helping in checking the diversion of food 
item under PDS to a large extent. They have also been asked to 
eliminate bogus ration cards and initiate action against erring FPS 
owners under section 3 of the Essential Commodities Acts, 1955.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION 
(SHRI SHRIRAM CHAUHAN): (a) and (b) The Public Distribution 
System (PDS) evolved as a system of management of scarcity and for 
distribution of foodgrains at affordable prices. Over the years, it has 
become an important part of Government's policy for management of 
food economy in the country. PDS is supplemental in nature and 
does not make available the entire requirement of any commodities 
to a household or section of the society. It is operated under the joint 
responsibility of the Central and State Governments. The Central 
Government is responsible for procurement, storage and 
transportation of PDS commodities up to the central godowns and 
making them available to the State Governments. The responsibility 
for distribution to the consumers th rough Fair Price Shops (FPSs) and, 
administration of PDS rests with State Governments/UT 
Administration. In order to e fficiently reach the essential 
commodities under Public Distribution System to the consumers 
in a transparent an d accountable manner a Model Citizens'

also     been     drawn     up     and     circulated     to     States/UTs     for

better safeguard food security co ncerns of all than the State 
bureaucracy, the Government has also advised the State 
Governments to more substantially involve the Gram Panchayats in 
supervision and moni† Oring of PDS especially at FPS level as a 
measure of social audit. 
State Governments have been requested to regularly monitor PDS 
at the Fair Price Shops (FPSs) and other levels and to make

appropriate action.

towards the 5% of the population who do not get even two square 
meals a day. The scheme contempl ates identificati on of one crore 
poorest "hungry" families and providing them with 25 kgs. of 
foodgrains per family per month at Rs. V- per kg. of Wheat and 
Rs. 3/- per kg. of rice.

Government has decided to decontrol the sugar industry in a

Income tax assessees and members of their families were 
excluded from the ' purview of the PDS levy sugar with 
effect from July, 2000. The supply of levy sugar under 
the PDS has been restricted, w ith effect from 1.2.2001, to 
the people below poverty line excep t in North-Eastern States/Hill 
States/Island Terri† Ories, wher e the existing arrangements would 
continue.  However, minimum per capita per month quantum of

The Department of Pension and Pensioners Welfare is the nodal

redressal of grievances of pensioners belonging to the Central 
Government Departments. Sanction, disbursement and settlement of 
pension cases of Central Government servants have been fully 
decentralised and individual Depart ments are responsible for sanction 
and disbursement of pension to their pensioners. Employees 
belonging to State Governments, public sector undertakings and 
autonomous institutions are governed by the pensionaryrctirement 
benefits as frameoVadopted by them. The CCS (Pension) Rules apply 
only to the Central Government servants. 
The Department of Pension an d Pensioners Welfare receives 
complaints from Central Government  pensioners as well as from the 
pensioners of various State Governments and autonomous 
institutions. While the Department of Pension and Pensioners 
Welfare facilities settlement of pensions belonging to Central 
Government, action to settle cases and redressal of grievances of 
pensioners belonging to the State Governments and their autonomous 
insitutions are to be considered by the respective State Governments 
and, therefore, complaints received from State Government 
pensioners are forwarded to the respective State Governments for 
their consideration. Necessary acti on has been taken in respect of 
complaints of both the above mentioned categories of pensioners in 
accordance with the existing procedure.

Upliftment of poor 
222. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as many as 2.8 billion people live 
below the poverty line with incomes averaging $2.00 a day; and 
(b) if so, what concrete steps are being taken by Government for 
the upliftment of the poor and raising their purchasing power? 
THE   MINISTER   OF   STATE   IN   THE   MINISTRY   OF 
PLANNING, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
STATISTICS AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI 
ARUN SHOURIE): (a) World Development Report, 2000-2001 
published by the World Bank has mentioned that of the world's 
6 billion people, 2.S billion live on less, than $2.00 a day. 
(b) There is a three-pronged ac tion to alleviate and reduce the 
poverty in the country. These ar e, : (i) acceleration of economic 
growth, (ii) human, and social development through literacy, 
education, health nutrition, meeting of the minimum needs, elevation" 
of social and economic status of th e weaker sections of the society, 
etc.. and (iii) direct attack on poverty through employment and 
income generating programmes and' assets-buiiding for the poor. 
The increase in income of the people living below the poverty 
line occurs from the joint impact of general growth process and direct 
income generation of the poor arising from various anti-poverty 
programmes introduced from time to time by the Government for 
their upliftment. Since the Sixth 0 Five Year Plan (1980—85), the 
Government has been implementing employment and asset 
generation schemes for the ur nent of the people living below the 
poverty line. These schemes are mainly of two types, self- 
employment and wage employment. Integrated Rural Development 
Programme (IRDP) has been the major self-employment programme 
and it has been in operation in all the blocks of the country since 
1980. The wage employment programme initially was National Rural 
Employment Programme (NREP) during the Sixth Plan period. In 
the Seventh Plan, another wage employment programme under the 
204 

[22 February, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
nanie Rural Labour Employment Guarantee Programme (RLEGP) 
was introduced. Then in 1989, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) was 
launched by merging the National Rural Employment Programme 
and the Rural Labour Employment Guarantee Programme, and it 
became the main wage-employment programme. In addition, several 
programmes to help the poor were also in operation until March, 
1999. These programmes are: Million Wells Scheme (MWS), 
Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS), Development of Women 
and Children in Rural Areas (DWCRA), Training of Rural Youth 
for Self-Employment (TRYSEM), Supply of Improved Toolkits to 
Rural Artisans (SITRA). 
From 1st April, 1999, these programmes, excepting EAS and 
JRY have been restructured into single self-employment programme 
called the Swarnayayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) with the 
primary objectives of focussed approach to poverty alleviation, 
capitalising advantages of group lending, and overcoming the 
problems associated with multiplicity of programmes. Also, from 
1st April, 1999, Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (JRY) has been 
restructured as Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana (JGSY) with the 
primary objective of creation of demand driven community village 
infrastructure including durable assets at the village level arid assets 
to enable the rural poor to increase the opportunities for sustained 
employment. Its secondary objective is generation of supplementary 
employment for the unemployed poor  in the-rural areas. The wage 
employment under the programme is given to Below Poverty Lines 
(BPL) families. 
From 1.12.1997, Swarna Jayanti Sahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) 
is the main poverty alleviation programme in the urban areas. The 
SJSRY, which has subsumed all the earlier three urban poverty 
alleviation programmes, viz., Nehru Rozgar Yojana (NRY), Urban 
Basic Services for the Poor (UBS P), Prime Minister's Integrated 
Urban Poverty Eradication Programme (PMIUPEP), seeks to 
provide gainful employment to unemployed or underemployed urban 
and educated up to IX standard for setting up self employment 
ventures or provision of wage employment. The implementation of 
SJSRY is relying on suitable community structures on the UBSP 
205 

RAJYA SABHA [22 February, 2001] 
pattern and delivery of inputs under this programme is through the 
medium of Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and such community 
structure.

pay" as contained in the aforementioned provisions of fundamental 
rules has also been affirmed by th e Supreme Court of India in respect 
of absence from duty due to strike.

Proposals on agriculture submitted to WTO 
*13. DR. MANMOHAN SINGH:  Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have submitted its proposals to WTO 
on agriculture for the ongoing negotiations; and 
(b) if so, the details of the signifi cant elements of  proposals to 
protect our agriculture? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) India has submitted its negotiating proposals in the areas of 
market access, domestic support , export competition and food 
security under the Agreement on Agriculture, to the WTO with the 
objective of protecting its food and livelihood security and creating 
increased market access opportun ities with a view to promote 
agricultural exports. 
The main elements of the proposals are: 
—  Additional flexibility for providing subsidies to key farm 
inputs for agricultural and rural development. 
—  Clarifications on certain im plementation issues, such as 
offsetting of positive non-product specific support with 
negative product specific support, suitable methodology of 
notifying domestic support in stable currency to take care of 
inflation and depreciation. 
—  Maintenance of appropriate level of tariff bindings on 
agricultural products in developing countries, keeping in mind 
  
 
225 
 

RAJYA SABHA [22 February, 2001] 
their developmental needs and high distortions prevalent in 
the international markets with a view to protect livelihood of 
their farming population. Also linking the appropriate levels 
of tariffs in developing countries with trade distortions in the 
areas of market access, dom estic support and export 
competition. 
—  Rationalisation of low tariff bindings in developing countries, 
which could not be rationalised in the earlier negotiations. 
—  Separate safeguard mechanisms on the lines of Special 
Safeguard Clause including a provision for imposition of 
quantitative Restrictions to protect the interest of the 
domestic producers in the event of a surge in imports or a 
decline in international prices , as a Special and Differential 
measure. 
—  No minimum market access co mmitments for developing 
countries. 
—  Measures taken by developing country members for 
alleviation of poverty, rural development, rural employment 
and diversification of agriculture should be exempt from any 
reduction commitments. 
—  Rationalisation of product coverage of Agreement on 
Agriculture (AoA) by inclusion of certain primary agricultural 
commodities such as rubber, jute, coir etc. 
—  Product specific support given to low income and resource 
poor farmers should also be excluded from the Aggregate 
Measurement of Support (AMS). 
—  Flexibility enjoyed by developing countries in taking certain 
measures in accordance with other WTO covered Agreements 
should not get constrained by the provisions of AoA. 
—  Substantial reduction in tariff bindings including elimination 
of peak tariffs and tariff escalations in developed countries, 
—  Expansion and transparent administration of Tariff Rate 
Quotas pending their eventual abolition. 
—  Blue box measures, de-coupled and direct payments, as well

Revision of Tariff on Chinese goods 
26. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Chinese goods arc flooding Indian markets; and  
(b) if so, the action taken to raise tariff to stop Chinese 
dumping? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): 
(a) and (b) A perusal of import data  reveals that there has not been 
any surge of import from China on an overall basis. The imports 
from China constitute on an average less than 3% of the total Indian 
imports. 
India and China have accorded Most Favoured Nation Status to 
262 

[22 February, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
each other as part of bilateral agreement. Thus, the import duties 
cannot be raised only on imports from China. However, the 
Government has received informa tion regarding dumping of some 
cheap consumer goods like dry batteries, sports shoes and toys from 
China. The Directorate Genral of Anti Dumping and Allied Duties 
has initiated proceedings against the import of these products on 
20.11.2000. Imposition of provisional anti-dumping duty has already 
been recommended in case of dry batteries and sports shoes. 
Flow of Chinese Goods into the Country 
27. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRL A: Will the Minister cf 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the large scale smuggling 
of inferior and sub-standard Chinese goods into the country's market 
through Nepal; 
(b) if so, what according to the a ssessment, if any, made by 
Government is the annual flow of Chinese sub-standard goods in the 
Indian market; and 
(c) what measures have been taken by Government to check it? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): 
(a) and (b) Smuggling being a clandestine activity, it is not possible to 
make any assessment about the quantum of smuggled goods. 
However, the intelligence and reports available do indicate smuggling 
of goods of Chinese origin into India through Indo-Nepal border. 
(c) All the field formations of the Customs Department including 
Directorate of Revenue Intelligence are on alert to detect and 
prevent smuggling of goods of Chinese origin. They have also been 
instructed to take stringent action against under invoicing of Chinese 
and other foreign goods. Further, steps have been taken to initiate 
the process of investigations to prevent dumping of Chinese goods 
into India.

basis of combined service rendered by them in the Government and 
BSNL.

Guidelines  for   Issue   of Licence   to   Infrastructure   Providers 
Category-II (IP-MI) 
The Infrastructure Providers Category-II (IP-II) are those 
Infrastructure Providers who lease rent outsell end to end bandwidth 
i.e. digital transmission capacity capable to carry a message. 
The following are the guidelines for issue of Licence for 
Infrastructure Providers Category I to be called IP-II. 
1. The applicant must be an Indi an company, registered under 
the Companies Act' 1956. 
2. The applicant company shall submit the application in the 
prescribed Application form for gr ant of a licence fo r Infrastructure 
Provider Category-II (IP-II) 
3. The foreign equity in the applicant company will not exceed 
49% at any time during the entire licence period. Investment in the 
equity of the applicant company by an NR/OCB/international 
funding agencies will be counted to wards its foreign equity. In this 
regard, the applicant company shall also submit a certificate from the

purpose of placing telegraph lines under Part III of the Indian 
Telegraph Act' 1885.

Provided further that the fee/ royalty for the use of spectrum

Austerity in Government Expenditure 
49. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will th e Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether with a view to bridging the widening deficit in the 
Budget, Government had adopted a comprehensive plan to enforce 
austerity in Government expenditure; 
(b) if so, the details of the austerity measures adopted thereunder 
and the economy so far affected thereby, item-wise indicating the 
saving in Government expenditure effected during 2000-2001, 
thereby; and 
(c) what further steps are contemplated in this direction? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
FINANCE (SHRI BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (c) It is 
Government's constant endeavour to contain non-plan, non- 
developmental expenditure. It is in this context that, alongwith 
other measures, instructions for austerity in Government 
expenditure have been issued from time to time. The austerity 
measures include ban on the creation of posts, reduction in the 
number of sanctioned post, restrictions on the filling up of vacant 
posts, reduction in office expenses, restrictions on purchase of 
vehicles, restrictions on foreign travel and on entertainment/ 
hospitality expenses etc. Considering the factors which contribute to 
the fiscal and revenue deficits, au sterity measures alone can have 
only a limited impact on the size of these deficits. As the 
information is not maintained centrally, it is not possible to quantify 
saving on account of issuance of economy instructions.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Operationalizing 'SARAS' 
* 41. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND 
ECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the prototype of "SARAS" reported to be an 
indigenously built multi purpose civili an aircraft, would be ready for 
take off by September, 2001; 
(b) if so, the special features of  the aircraft and how does it 
compare with other similar aircraft in the world on standard 
parameters of technology, cost etc.; and 
(c) the time schedule drawn up for its commercial production? 
THE MINISTER FOR HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
AND MINISTER OF SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY 
(DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to  (c) A statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) All efforts are being made to undertake the first test flight of 
the prototype of 'SARAS' by September/October, 2001. 
(b) The SARAS aircraft is powered by two turbo prop engines of 
850 SHP (PT6A-66) in a pusher configuration with variable pitch 
propellers. It has a maximum speed of about 500 km/h and can fly 
upto 30000 ft. altitude and has an endurance of 6 hours. Maximum 
all-up-weight is 6100 Kg. and the aircraft can accommodate 14 
passengers in the standard version. 
SARAS is suitable for short hops in the commuter role as well as 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [23 February, 2001] 
long range high speed cruise in the executive transport version. It can 
be used for aerial ambulance, as co ast guard/border surveillance, in 
disaster management, etc. The Aircraft has following features: all 
weather, day/night flight capability; operability from high altitude 
airfields on hot days with little or no compromise on take-off weight; 
pressurized cabin; composite control surfaces: cabin comfort level 
matching that of regional aircraft; fully duplicated flight deck, etc. 
The existing aircraft are designed to US FAR-23 standards 
(1970 technology) whereas SARAS is based on US FAR-25 standards 
(Amendment 1991) with enhanced safety requirements (for e.g. seats 
are designed to meet 16g dynamic load  etc.). The cost of an imported 
aircraft of this category such as Beech King Air is in the range of 
US $ 4*5 millions against the cost of SARAS produced indigenously is 
estimated to be in the range of US $ 3.75 millions and all efforts are 
being made to reduce it further. Furthermore, the operating costs of 
SARAS will be lower by about 20% in comparison to similar other 
aircrafts. 
(c) HAL is the major partner of the SARAS developmental 
programme and it has the first right to series production. Private 
industries will also participate. It is expected that the aircraft will be 
type certified by the middle of 2003 . Based on the te chno-commercial 
evaluation, commercial production schedule will be drawn up.

Extinction threat to bird species 
* 42. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Bombay Natural Hist ory Society and Bird Life 
International have cautioned that the number of bird species 
threatened with extinction in India is rising at an alarming rate; 
(b) whether these bodies have stated  that endangered birds, which 
need to be protected, are pink, headed duck, forest owlet, jerdon's 
courser, Himalayan mountain qualis, Sarus, crane and two species of 
vultures; and 
(c) if so, what steps Government are taking to protect these birds? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS 
(SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the Table of 
the House. 
Statement 
(a) Several organizations including Bombay Natural History 
Society, Bird Life International have been expressing 
concerns about decline in population of several bird species 
in India. 
(b) Pink headed duck and the Himalayan mountain quail were 
last sighted in 1935 and 1876 respectively. These birds are 
since considered extinct. Jerdon's  courser was also considered 
extinct, but was rediscovered by Bombay Natural History 
Society in Cuddapah Region of Andhra Pradesh in 1986. The 
State Government has notified the crucial habitat of the 
species as Sri Lankamalleswara Sanctuary for providing 
effective protection to the species. 
Forest Spotted Owlet (Anthene bl ewitti) is also a rare species 
of bird, which is endemic to Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya 
Pradesh and Orissa. Very little information is available about 
current status of the species. Bombay Natural History Society 
is conducting "Ecological Studies" on this species. 
Although  Saras  Crane  is not  a species threatened with 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [23 February, 2001] 
extinction, there has been decline of population of this 
species due to decrease in the number and extent of wet 
lands, use of chemical fertilizer s, pesticides and chemically 
treated seeds. 
There has also been a sharp decline in the population of 
different species of vultures. An International workshop was 
organized by Bombay Natural History Society with the 
support of Central Government to take stock of current 
situation and evolve an effective strategy for the conservation 
of vultures. The main recommendation of the Workshop are 
as follows:—  
(i) Need for survey of vultures throughout the country. 
(ii) Study ecological and environmental factors respon- 
sible for decline of vultures population. 
(Hi) Disease and Toxicological studies among the sick 
vultures. 
(iv) Ex-situ conservation measures. 
(c) Some of the impotant steps taken by the Central Government 
to protect Jerdon's Courser, Forest Spotted Owlet, Sarus, 
Crane and Vultures are as follows:—  
(i) Hunting of all wild animals and birds has been 
banned under Wildlife (Protection) Act. 
(ii) Crucial habitats of various species of wild animals 
and birds have been notified as national parks and 
sanctuaries. Important national parks and sanctuaries 
are also notified as Ramsar Sites and World Natural 
Heritage Sites. 
(iii) Regular patrolling of the area to control poaching 
and illegal trade in wild animals and their products is 
done. Cooperation of other enforcement agencies and 
international organizations is also taken in this 
regard.

Smt. Shabana Azmi, has already mentioned about the purpose. I do 
not want to repeat it. The purpose is to create a knowledge-based 
society; and, at the end, the Repor t says that it is to create a 
competitive environment. Sir, I take your point that a knowledge- 
based society is important. But knowledge for whom? Is it only for a 
selected few? There is a very in teresting and, really, an almost 
frightening sentence in this Report . It is, 'India currently faces two 
challenges — income poverty and information poverty. The two 
challenges have to be equally met.' How do you equate the two? Of 
course, knowledge is important. Though I have spent all my life in 
the field of education, I cannot equate knowledge poverty with 
poverty of food, drinking water and housing. Would the hon. 
Minister accept this view? 
The second question is this. Sir, much has been said about 
privatisation. What would be the affect of privatisation of higher 
education? The Report says, "leave..." — not party — "... higher 
and professional education to private sector." If the entire education 
is left to the private sector, which ultimately increases the cost of 
education, what will be the effect on women in a highly patriarchal 
society? Does it not amount to is empowerment *rf women? 
DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: Sir, I have made it amply clear 
that this Report is under consideration and the Government will take 
24 

[23 February, 2001]        RAJYA SABHA 
a final view after taking into account the views of the hon. Members 
of the House, the views of educa tionists and the views of all those 
who have a stake in education. So, there should be no apprehension 
about it. 
Secondly, I am repeating ad nauseam that the Government has full 
commitment for the socially deprived sections of the people and, 
particularly, for women. The Government has a policy of making 
education free for all women up  to graduation and also for 
professional courses for the SC/ST girls. So, our commitment for 
women and for these sections is fully amplified by our policy 
statements. But, please do not be scared. If somebody wants to help 
or some institution wants to help our educational system, should we 
take it or should we not take it? Should the Indian universities 
remain starved of funds totally? Or, should we make use of the 
opportunity offered by those donors, as I have said, who are here to 
help their alma mater. We are considering all these aspects and we 
will take into account to see that  any education policy does not 
deprive anybody who is meritorious and poor with regard to access to 
higher education upto the highest level. 
Secondly, we fully agree that there is a role for the Government at 
all levels of education, be it primar y, be it higher, be it research or 
be it technology.

Reforms ln technical education 
† * 56. SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
 DR. D. MASTHAN: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that ther e is a need for comprehensive 
reform in technical education in the country; 
(b) if so, whether Government have prepared any draft scheme for 
the said reforms; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and what decision has been taken by 
Government for getting assistance from private sector to implement 
this scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT 
(DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (c) "Reforms in technical 
education in the country is a continuous process and this is achieved 
through the implementation of the National Policy on Education 
(NPE) and the Programme of Action (PoA). It includes coordinated 
and planned development of technical education as embodied in the 
All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE) Act, 1987. 
For the development of technical education, AICTE runs several 
schemes such as Modernisation and Removal of Obsolescence, 
Thrust Area Programme in Tec hnical Education, Research and 
Development Programme, Entrepreneurship and Management 
Development Programme, Early Faculty Induction Programme, Quality

52 

[23 February, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Improvement Programme, strengthening of National Board of 
Accreditation, etc. An All India Boar d of IT Education has also been 
constituted under AICTE. 
Apart from the initiatives on the part of the AICTE, recent 
initiatives taken to strengthen the technical education system include 
strengthening and consolidation of infrastructural facilities in Indian 
Institutes of Technology (IITs), I ndian Institutes of Management 
(IIMs), Indian Institute of Scie nce (IISc), Regional Engineering 
Colleges (RECs) etc; establishment of more IITs, IIMs and 
Engineering Colleges; establishment of Indian Institute of 
Information Technology (HIT) at A llahabad and Indian Institute of 
Informantion Technology & Management (IIITM) at Gwalior; 
National Programme for HRD in IT, Review of Postgraduate 
Education; increase of students in take in engineering and technical 
institutions; increasing output of information technology manpower; 
mobilization of privat e initiatives; developmen t of technologies in 
emerging areas and their transfer to user agencies through technology 
development missions; transfer of techno-economic advances in 
technical education and appropriate technologi es to rural people 
through expansion of Community Polytechnics; Scheme for upgrading 
existing polytechnics to integrate the physically disabled in the main 
stream of technical and vocational education; modernisation of 
institutions and development of R&D base; Technician Education 
Project; modernisation of libraries and switch over to electronic 
libraries with interconnectivity; etc.  RECs are being strengthened as 
per the Mashelkar Committee recommendations to become world 
class institutions (Centres of Excellence). Furthermore, technical 
education system will also work for improving the productivity of the 
informal sector of the economy. 
Private Sector is involved substantially in running of technical 
institutes, some of which are of very good quality, under the overall 
supervision of AICTE."

Ash Pond Accident at NALCO 
*57.  SHRI V.P. DURAISAMY: 
SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: 
Will the Minister of MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that National Aluminium Company Ltd. 
Orissa has two large ash ponds; 
(b) whether one of these ponds developed a breach of 
embankment on Dec. 31, 2000, resulting in sudden flooding of the 
villages down the stream of Nadira rivulet; 
(c) if so, the extent of damage caused to the people, plants and 
water of the region, indicating th e loss of life and property, the 
amount of compensation paid by NALCO; and 
(d) the cause of the accident and whet her there is apprehension of 
similar accident in NALCO? 
THE MINISTER OF MINES (SHRI SUNDAR LAL PATWA): 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) There is no loss of life and personal property except for some 
damage of crops. District Authorities constituted several Committees 
to assess the loss of or damage to property, crops, and soil condition, 
as also to assess the restoration measures required in the area. The 
Collector reviewed the progress of relief and restoration measures 
undertaken in the affected villages. He conducted a meeting which 
was attended by local MPs, MLAs, Zilla Parishad Members, 
Sarpanch and other public repr esentatives, officials of State 
Government and NALCO officials, where issues relating to water 
supply, compensation for crops, damage/loss to the property, 
removal of ash from the land, reclamation of Government land and 
repair and renovation of damaged infr astructure etc. were deliberated 
upon and on receipt of consensus view of the public representatives 
54 

[23 February, 2001]        RAJYA SABHA 
and Government officials, the Collector, Angul recommended an 
amount of Rs. 1121.76 lakhs for immediate payment. This amount 
includes compensation and developmental work and will be paid 
directly to District Ad ministration for settlement of claims to the 
ultimate beneficiaries against individual acknowledgement. 
(d) In order to assess the cause of accident, Ministry of Mines has 
constituted an independent Committee headed by an Executive 
Director, NTPC. One internal Commi ttee has also been constituted 
by NALCO to find out the cause of  accident. The Reports of the two 
Committees are expected by end of February, 2001. The experts from 
Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore have examined both ash ponds 
of NALCO. The required repairs, reconstruction and strengthening 
wroks as per the suggestion and advice of these Scientists have been 
taken up. In view of this, there is no apprehension of another similar 
accident.

Production cost of urea in private sector 
 
† 225. SHRI   BRATIN   SENGUPTA:   Will   the   Minister   of 
CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) the existing cost of urea in priv ate sector and the reasons for 
the high cost; 
(b) whether Government propose to reduce the production cost 
of urea; and 
(c) if not, the reasons theretor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI SATYA BRATA 
MOOKHERJEE): (a) Under Retentio n Price-cum-Subsidy Scheme, 
the retention prices (cost of production plus 12% post tax return) are 
fixed unit-wise having regard to a combination of norms and actuals 
of various cost elements. Operational cost of production of urea units 
differs not only from unit to unit but also from month to month, 
depending upon, inter-alia, the health and vintage of the plant, the 
feedstock used, the level of capacity  utilization, specific consumption 
and inputs eost. Such computation is not related to *he unit being in 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
72 

[23 February, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
private or in cooperative/public  sector. However, the weighted 
average retention price of urea units in private sector is Rs. 9764 per 
MT as compared to that of Rs. 8166 per MT in respect of all urea 
units, as on 1.4.2000. 
The main reasons for high cost of production in private sector 
are two-fold. Firstly, of the 12 ureas producing units in private sector, 
7 are naphtha based units whose cost of production is higher than the 
all-unit average on account of high cost of feed stock i.e. naphtha. 
Secondly, the remaining 5 units are gas based but have been 
commissioned after 1991 except Indo-Gulf Corporation, Jagdishpur 
and thereby have comparatively higher capital related charges. 
(b) and (c) Installation of energy  saving measures such as Purge 
Gas Recovery (PGR) unit etc. and promoting technological 
improvement for improving energy ef ficiency in urea units are some 
of the measures taken by the Government towards reducing the 
retention price of urea units.

CAG Report on Clean Ganga Project 
239. SHRI NARENDRA MOHAN: 
SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: 
SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: 
Will the Minister of ENVI RONMENT AND FORESTS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Comptroller and Auditor 
General of India has recently decl ared in his Report that the 
Grandiose Clean Ganga Project has failed to achieve its objective 
despite an expenditure of over Rs. 900 crore in the past 15 years and 
that quality of Ganga water, as also its tributaries has actually 
deteriorated further since 1993; 
(b) if so, whether the National River Conservation Authority, 
and Ministry of Environment and Forests are thinking of fixing the 
responsibility for this state of affairs and issuing further guidelines to 
ensure effective and timely implem entation of Clean Ganga Project; 
and 
(c) what action Government are ta king on the CAG report to 
ensure that there is not further wa stage and the objectiv es of the Plan 
are achieved? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS 
(SHRI T.R. BAALy): (a) to (c) The Comptroller and Auditor 
General (CAG) of India in his report on Ganga Action Plan for the 
year ended March, 2000 has covered the review of performance of 
Ganga Action Plan Phase I and Gang a Action Plan Phase II. As for 
the Ganga Action Plan Phase I wh ich was started in 1985, the 
programme has been declared clos ed as on 31.3.2000 and a total 
expenditure of Rs. 452  crore has been incurred on it. Under this 
Plan, a capacity to treat 835 milli on litres per day of sewage and 
other facilities like low cost toilets, crematoria, bathing ghats etc. 
have been created. Certain problems of operation and maintenance 
of the assets have emerged in Bihar and to some extent in Uttar 
Pradesh. The matter is being constantly persued with these State 
88 

[23 February, 2001]        RAJYA SABHA 
Governments at the highest level. As for the Ganga Action Plan 
Phase II, this programme was approv ed in three stages form 1993 to 
1996. The Plan covers pollution abatement works in 95 towns along 
the Ganga and its tributaries namely, Yamuna, Gomti, and 
Damodar. The approved cost of the Plan is Rs. 1276.26 core. A total 
capacity of about 1861 million litres per day of sewage treatment 
alongwith allied works is to be created under this Flan. 
The implementation of Plan has delayed due to the following 
reasons: 
(i) The scheme of National River Conservation Plan of which 
Ganga Action Plan Phase II is a part, was originally 
envisaged on 50:50 cost sharing basis between Centre and 
States. However, in view of the difficulties of the State 
Governments in bringing their 50% share, the National River 
Conservation Authority under the Chairmanship of Prime 
Minister at its 9th Meeting held in July, 1997 converted the 
scheme into a 100% Centrally Funded Scheme. But the 
Cabinet approval to this decision could be obtained only in 
November, 1998. During the intervening period of 16 
months, the States were not providing their share in 
anticipation that the scheme will become 100% Centrally 
funded. As a result, the progre ss of the scheme became very 
slow. 
(ii) The convention technologies proposed earlier'did not address 
the problem of bacterial pollution fully. In order to address 
this issue, a decision was taken in July, 1999 to adopt 
oxidation pond based sewage treatment in all the places. 
These ponds, although requiring large areas of land are 
capable of reducing fecal coliform suitably. The State 
Governments could not provide such areas of land of larger 
towns which account for major chunk of the capital cost. As 
a result, the progress of work was extremely slow for nearly 
18 months. 
(iii) Until   1999-2000,   grants   were .released   to   the   State 
89 

RAJYA SABHA [23 February, 2001] 
Governments. Transfer of such grants to the implementing 
agencies were invariably delaye d in almost all the States for 
a period ranging from 6-9 months affecting the progress of 
work adversely. 
(iv) The quality of preparation of Detailed Project Reports was 
not up to the mark from a number of State which resulted in 
significant delays. 
(v) There were delays in land acquisition in Uttar Pradesh and 
West Bengal. 
(vi) Decision was taken by the Ministry not to release funds for 
Ganga Action Plan Phase II in  Bihar because the operation 
and maintenance of assets created under Ganga Action Plan 
Phase II was not satisfactory. 
As a result, a capacity of 634 milli on litres per day of sewage has 
been commissioned so far. The aforesaid bottlenecks have now been 
resolved and the Plan is now targetted to be completed by 2005. Thus 
the impact of the Action Plan on the improvement of water quality of 
rivers and achievement of objectiv es can be expected only after 
completion of the Plan.

Review of TB eradication programme 
255. SHRI A. VIJAYA RAGHAVAN : Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made any review regarding the Tuberculosis 
eradication programmes with the assistance of international agencies; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government would review the functioning of the existing 
programmes according to the convenience of poor patients; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
110 

[23 February, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA):  (a) National TB 
Control Programme (NTCP) was reviewed in 1992 by an Expert 
Committee consisting of National and International experts. 
Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) was reviewed 
in February, 2000 jointly by Government of India and WHO. 
Subsequently, the programme was reviewed by World Bank in 
September, 2000. 
(b) The main conclusions of the 1992 review of NTCP are as 
under: 
• Less than 40% patients completed treatment. 
• Inadequate budget and insufficient managerial capacity. 
• Shortage of drugs. 
• Emphasis on X-ray diagnosis resulting in inaccurate diagnosis. 
• Poor quality smear microscopy. 
• Multiplicity of treatment regimen. 
Joint review of RNTCP by WHO and Government of India found 
that programme was being successfully implemented in the country 
with accurate diagnosis and regu lar and uninterrupted supply of 
drugs. The review by World Bank recommended for great 
decentralization of the programme and ownership by States. 
(c) and (d) Under the National TB Control Programme (NTCP), 
cash assistance is provided by the Central Government for 100% 
requirement of anti-TB drugs for sputum negative cases and anti-TB 
drugs are provided in kind for the sputum positive cases, to all the 
States for all district s except those covered under RNTCP. Under the 
Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP), which has an 
objective of coverage of at least 85% new, smear positive cases and 
detecting at least 70% of such cas es, anti-TB drugs are provided in 
kind for both sputum negative and sputum positive patients in all the 
districts covered under RNTCP. This programme, which is at present 
covering about 330 million population, has a cure rate of above 85%.

small pox which had become almost extinct, are taking place again;

almost the same throughout the country. 
In so far as Malaria is concerned,  the incidence of malaria in the 
country was brought down to the leve l of 0.1 million cases annually in 
1965 which resurged and increased to  6.47 million cases annually in 
1976. The incidence was again brought down to 2.18 million cases in 
the year 1984 and since then it has been contained around 2-3 million 
cases annually. The areas most affected by malaria are seven North- 
Eastern States and predominant by tribal areas of the States of 
Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Jharkhand,

Norms for clinical trials of drugs 
263. SHRI SANJAY NIRUPAM: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) wheiher Government are aware of the proposal mooted by the 
R&D Sub-Committee of CII's National Committee on Drugs and 
Pharmaceuticals, seeking changes in nor ms for clinical trials of drugs 
in the country; if so, the details thereof; 
(b) the salient features of existing norms of clinical trials; and 
(c) whether Government propose to amend the existing norms, on 
the basis of suggestions so received; if so, by when? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) No such proposal 
has been received. 
(b) At present clinical trials in the country are governed by the 
provisions contained in Schedule Y of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 
and Rules thereunder. The level of clinical trials required to be 
carried out before a new drug is approved for manufacture/marketing 
depends to an extent on the status of that drug in other countries. 
If it has been already approved for manufacture or marketing and 
adequate documentation regarding the clinical trials done in that 
connection is available, then only Phase III trials, as laid down in 
Schedule Y of the Drug and Cosmetics Rules is required. 
If the drug has not been approved elsewhere, then trials are 
118 

[23 February, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
generally  required  from  a  level  previous  to  the  phase  of trial 
underway in other countries. 
For new drug substances discovered in other countries, Phase I 
trials are not usually allowed to be initiated in India, unless 
Phase I data relating to human/clinical pharmacology is available, 
exemption in this regard is ava ilable in cases where the drug has 
a special relevance in this country in terms of public health. 
New drug substances discovered in this country need to 
undertake clinical trials right from Phase I. 
(c) To streamline the process of conducting clinical trials of 
drugs and their clearance Government have inter alia taken the 
following measures:—  
(1) A committee of experts has been set  up vide order dated 
17.01.2001 which also spells out the modalities for 
processing   applications   relating   to investigational   new 
drugs. 
(2) Guidelines relating to Good Clinical Practices |(GCP) are 
also being finalised for early publication.

T.B. incidence 
275. SHRI CO. POULOSE: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) The incidence of tuberculosis re ported in the country, State- 
wise; 
(b) the factors behind increasing incidence of TB; and 
(c) what steps Government have taken against the incidence and in 
the matter of TB drugs resistance? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) The incidence TB cases in 
the country is estimated to be 225 per lakh of population. 
The State-wise cases correspond to their population accordingly. 
(b) the trend of tuberculosis in India over last several years has 
been more of less static. About 1.2 million fresh TB cases are 
reported every year in the county; 
(c) Government of India has introduced the Revised National TB 
Control programme (RNTCP) which aims at coverage of at least 85% 
new smear positive cases and detecting at least 70% of such cases. 
Under this Programme, which is at present covering about 330 
million population a cure rate of 85%, has been achieved. 
Drug resistant TB is the outcome of poor programme performance 
and arises due to improper/irregular /incomplete treatment. It is the 
policy of the Government of India to control MDR TB by stopping at 
its inception by ensuring that patients take complete and proper 
treatment. For this purpose, the Di rectly Observed Treatment Short 
Course (DOTS) Strategy has been adopted under RNTCP under 
which patient-wise boxes of anti-TB drugs for the complete treatment 
are supplied and medicines have to be taken by the patients under 
the direct supervision of the DOTS provider.

319. SHRI ANANTRAY DEVSHANKER DAVE: 
SHRI BRATIN SENGUPTA: 
Will the Minister of MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that Mineral deposits in Bihar 
and Gujarat are not being exploited properly; 
(b) if so, whether Government have formulated any plan in this 
regard; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether any financial assistance has been provided by 
Government to exploit these deposits during the last two years; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof, year-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF MINES 
(SHRI JAYSINGRAO GAIKWAD PATIL): (a) to (c) As per 
information available with the Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM), a 
subordinate office of the Ministry of Mines, the mineral deposits of 
Bihar viz. limestone, mica, pyrites, quartzite and steatite are being 
223 

RAJYA SABHA [23 February, 2001] 
exploited. The mineral deposits in Gujarat viz. bauxite, chalk, 
dolomite, fireclay, limestone, kaolin, silica sand and lignite are being 
exploited on a large scale. The numb er of mines, mineral-wise in the 
States of Bihar and Gujarat as per the information available with 
IBM is given in the Statement (See below). 
Government of India had announced the National Mineral Policy, 
1993 for development of mining sector in India including the States of 
Bihar and Gujarat. The Mines and Minerals (Development and 
Regulation) Act, 1957 was amended in January, 1994 and 
subsequently in December, 1999 followed by amendments in the 
Rules framed under the Act to make the legal framework investor 
friendly and hassle free. Similarly the policy for encouraging private 
sector investments including foreign direct investment has been 
increasingly liberalised over the years. 
(d) and (e) Any Indian National or a Company as defined in sub- 
section (1) of Section 3 of the Companies Act, 1956 is free to exploit 
the mineral reserves after getting a mining lease in accordance with 
the provisions of Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) 
Act, 1957 and Rules framed thereunder. No financial assistance is 
provided by the Central Government to exploit the mineral deposits.

Task Force for investment flow in the Railways 
321. SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ: Will the Minister of 
RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in order to plan flow of investment from non- 
traditional sources of revenue, a Task Force was set up; 
(b) if so, the details of their recommendations; 
(c) whether Empowered Committees were formed to expedite 
issue of guidelines; and 
(d) the details of the guidelines issued to Zonal Railways? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
RAILWAYS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. In 
order to plan flow of investment from noo-traditional sources of 
revenue, a Task Force comprising senior Railway Officers and 
representatives from FICCI, Cll a nd ASSOCHAM was set up to 
undertake an in-depth study of various issues. The Task Force has 
recommended generating revenues from non-traditional sources like 
commercial utilization of land and air space, Own Your Wagon 
226 

[23 February, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Scheme, BOLT (Build-Own-Lease-Transfer) Scheme, commercial 
publicity and other innovative financing packages including joint 
ventures and formation of SPVs (Special Purpose Vehicles) with 
private organisations. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir and the following actions have been taken; 
(i) Comprehensive guidelines have been issued to all the Zonal 
Railways for improving earnings from Commercial Publicity. The 
guidelines cover station premises, trai ns, level crossing, approaches to 
the major stations etc. In each ar ea of activity, the action to be taken 
by the Zonal Railways have been spelt out. 
(ii) The detailed methodology for commercial use of railway land/ 
air space has been issued to all Z onal Railways and the railways have 
been asked to take up the sites identified. 
(iii) A new corporation has been set up to: 
—commercially exploit the Right of Way of the Railways along 
railway track for laying of optical fiber cable. 
(iv) Introduction of "Own Your  Wagon" scheme. Its success, 
however, depends upon various factors like wagon availability in 
general, state of economy, demand for transport, cost of capital etc. 
In order to bring the financing of the scheme in line with the 
prevailing money market conditions, the payment of lease charges has 
been linked to prime lending rate, depreciation benefit and corporate 
tax instead of a fixed rate for the entire contract period.

Favour to MNCs by the Railways 
328. SHRIMATI CHANDRA KALA PANDEY: Will the 
Minister of RAILWAY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to a news- 
item "Railways Scheme favours MN C" appearing in the Times of 
India' Kolkata dated 19th January, 2001; and 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
RAILWAYS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) and (b) to 
proliferate retail railway ticketing through the use of Service 
Providers and terminal operators so th at there is a saving in the cost 
for the railways and improvement in customer interface process, 
Indian Railways has entered into an MoU with Indian Railway 
catering & Tourism Corporation Ltd. (IRCTC) to facilitate railway 
ticketing. IRCTC in turn will appoint Service Providers to give them 
IT support in the form of hardware , software and the technology and 
finance. The terminal operators may also be appointed in India and 
abroad to facilitate ticketing. As the volume of traffic on Indian 
Railways is quite large, it has been decided to invite offers only from 
those parties who have wide experience in this field and are 
technically and financially very sound. Inicidentally, most of the 
companies short-listed are Indian Companies or Consortium of Indian

RAILWAYS (SHRI DIGVUAY SINGH): (a) to (d) Upgradation of

system is a continuous and need based exercise which takes into 
account the availability of resources and requirements of the system 
for upgrading its services and for ensuring better safety standards.

Resource constraints do, however, exist. Efforts continue to be 
made with the Planning Commission and Ministry of Finance in this

Thefts in Railway Bogies 
338. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Will the Minister of 
RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that thefts in Railway Bogies during transit 
are increasing; 
(b) whether there is any plan to use temper free locks for each 
bogiy; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
RAILWAYS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) No. Sir. There is no 
increase in theft from Railway Bogies (Wagons) over Railways. 
(b) and (c) Adequate locking arrangement already exists on all 
covered wagons. After closing the doors, arrangement is available to 
seal the flaps and also pad lock the same, if required. The present 
locking system is considered adequate  and at present there is no plan 
to adopt any other tamper free locking system. 
(d) The existing locking arrangement is considered adequate. There 
is no possibility of pilferage if the wagon doors are locked and sealed

Manipulation of Rail Accident Statistics 
373. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: W ill the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Railway Board has noted that one factor 
bedevilling the safety performance of the Railways has been the wide- 
spread manipulation of accident statistics; 
(b) if so, the facts and figures on the basis of which the Railway 
Board has come to this conclusion and how far manipulation of 
accident statistics affected the safety performance; and 
(c) the steps taken and being taken to rectify the system and to 
bring about a reliable safety environment? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
RAILWAYS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to (c) No, Sir. There 
is no manipulation of Railway accide nt statistics. Various types of 
accidents are reported to differe nt levels depending on their 
seriousness. Yard derailments etc. are reported only upto the level of 
Divisions. Smaller acci dents not having seri ous repercussions are 
reported only upto the level of Zonal Railways. Only 'Consequential 
Train Accidents' which include collisions, derailment, level crossing 
accidents and fire cases having serious repercussions are reported to 
Railway Board. Thus, it is a matter of reporting at different levels for 
different accidents depending on their seriousness. 
Demand and supply of Oilzapper 
374. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the present demand and, supply position of Oilzapper in 
the country; 
293 

RAJYA SABHA [23 February, 2001] 
(b) what are the prospects of its exports; 
(c) whether any MoU has been signed with foreign countries/ 
companies; and 
(d) if so, the details in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) 
Oilzapper is carrier based efficient crude oil and oily sludge degrading 
bacterial consortia. Oilzapper can be  packed in poly bags and easily 
transported to the sites of refinery or accidental crude oil spill sites. 
Indian Oil refineries are generating around 20,000 metric tonnes of 
oily sludge, per annum. To degrade 20,000 metric tonnes of oily 
sludge, 200 metric tonnes of Oil zapper is required. In addition, 
around 100 metric tonnes of Oilzap per will be required to clean-up 
contaminated sites due to oil spills. Hence, the total expected annual 
demand of Oilzapper is 300 metric tonnes for indigenous 
requirement. 
At present, commercial production of Oilzapper has not started. 
The research laboratory is producing about 10 tonnes per annum for 
demonstration purpose. 
(b) The export potential of Oilzapper is quite high. Malaysia, 
Singapore, China and Saudi Arabia have shown interest in the 
product. 
(c) No MoU has been signed with foreign countries/companies. 
(d) Not applicable.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Safety Measure in Housing Projects 
*61. SHRI R. MARGABANDU: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Central Government Employees Welfare 
Housing Organisation (CGEWHO) has undertaken several housing projects all 
over the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether adequate safety measures are adopted by the organisation to 
prevent any damage or loss to the property due to natural calamities; 
(d) if so, the details thereof, and if not, the reasons therefor; 
(e) whether Government have issued any guidelines/instructions to the 
organisation to implement the necessary safety standards in the wake of the 
recent earthquake in Gujarat; and 
(f) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION (SHRI JAGMOHAN): (a) to (f) A Statement is laid on the Table 
of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. CGEWHO has undertaken 15 projects till date. Details are 
given in Statement-I. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. All the projects have been designed and built in 
accordance with the relevant  codal provisions as formulated by Bureau of 
Indian Standard (BIS) which cater to the effects of earthquake and wind forces. 
The details are indicated in Statement-II.

Statement-II 
Details of Earthquake Resistant Design 
EARTHQUAKE FORCES: As per IS Code 1893, whole country is divided 
into 5 zones dipending on the intensity of earthquake force expected during the 
occurrence. For example. Delhi falls inZone-IV, Kolkata& Mumbai in Zone-Ill, 
Chennai in Zone-II and Bangalore in Zone-I whereas Ahmedabad falls in Zone-
Ill. All structures are required to be designed to withstand earthquake forces 
relevant to the particular zone. 
WIND FORCES: As in case of earthquake, whole country is divided into 
various wind pressure zones depending on the wind intensity expected during 
the high winds/cyclone. For example, maximum wind pressure for Delhi is 60 kg

from Gujarat to Mumbai the same is 150 kg/sqmt. and from Mumbai to

withstand the wind forces relevant the particular zone. 
DESIGN OF BUILDINGS: Design of buildings is carried out for severe affect

SHRI R. MARGABANDU: Sir, collapse of buildings due to substandard 
construction and inadequate safety meas ure experienced in the recent earth-
quake suggests that structural engineers, contractors and officials who certify 
the fitness of buildings should be made accountable. I want to know whether 
the Government has got any proposal to amend the Structural Engineers Act 
and the Indian Architects Act. If so, what are the proposed amendments and 
their possible effects? 
SHRI JAGMOHAN: Sir, there is already an Indian Architects Act. On the 
lines of this Act, we are trying to frame an Indian Engineers Act which will 
cover all types of engineers, including structural engineers. Similar Acts are 
being administered by the Ministry of Human Resource Development. We have 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [26th February, 2001] 
suggested to them that there should be an enactment of this nature so that the 
professional conduct of the engineers can be regulated and controlled. If any 
structural engineer does not do his job properly, or, gives a false certificate, or, 
does not follow the building bye-laws and the codes prescribed in this regard, 
then he can be hauled up for professional misconduct and his registration or 
his licence could be cancelled. That is the provision. 
SHRI R. MARGABANDU: I want to know whether there is a proposal to 
amend these two Acts. 
SHRI JAGMOHAN: Sir, as I said, the Indian Architects Act already exists. 
But in regard to structural engineers, there is no Act. Now, it is proposed to be 
framed. 
SHRI R. MARGABANDU: Sir, I want to know whether the Government is 
aware that with the amount allotted for hundred per cent work, they actually carry 
out only 50 per cent work, after making deductions by way of percentage 
commission to the officials who issue fitn ess certificate for claim, to different 
agencies and contractors' dividend. It results in substandard and unsafe 
construction which collapse at any time causing loss of life and damage to 
property even when there is no earthquake. 
The second part of my supplementary is this. A tender is accepted of the 
lowest bid even when it is less than 10 to 15 per cent of the estimated tender 
price. Will it be allowed in future? If so, how will the standard of building be 
ensured? 
SHRI JAGMOHAN: Sir, even according to the normal rules, the norms of 
structural safety are not compromised while accepting or rejecting the tenders. The 
tender is to be within the framework of  the bye-laws, it has to be within the 
framework of the law. So, there can't be any compromise with regard to these 
building bye-laws. Therefore, that apprehension is not well-based. 
So far as somebody issuing a false certificate or using less material is 
concerned, that is, of course, an offence; it is corruption. You have seen action 
taken in a number of cases. Even in Delhi, some cases have been registered and 
action under criminal laws is taken wherever it is detected. 
SHRI S.B. CHAVAN: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would like to have a reply from 
the hon. Minister on two points. One is the standards which have been followed so 
far. It depends on the code of 1893. For almost a hundred years, in zone 3, there 
was, practically, no serious earthquake taking place. But after the Koyna 
4 

[26th February, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
earthquake, the Latur earthquake and th e recent one in Gujarat, the Bhuj 
earthquake, the matters have to be reconsidered. In the case of buildings and 
irrigation projects—which are there in those areas, whether they have been 
constructed or under construction-does the Government think it necessary to 
revise the instructions to all the officers who are incharge of construction of 
these buildings or irrigation projects? They need to be revised so as to take the 
earthquake factor into account, especially in the case of multi-storeyed buildings

SHRI JAGMOHAN: Sir, the position is like this. There is a Bureau of Indian 
Standard based on this. The National Building Code there is updated from time to 
time. The present code is quite updated. We, in the Ministry, have published a 
vulnerability atlas, which shows the vulnerability of all the areas; whether they 
are vulnerable to earthquakes, cyclones or floods. The degree or vulnerability 
has also been defined. For example, in the case of earthquakes, we have got five 
zones. Zone-5 is most prone to earthquake, like Bhuj. Then there are areas which 
are not so much prone, but, still, the degree is only slightly less. There are zene-
4 areas like Delhi. Delhi falls in that category. Zone 3 is still less prone. Ahmedabed 
falls in zone-3. Zone-2 and zone-1 are not so much vulnerable and the danger that 
can be caused can't be so much. So, the National Building Code of the Bureau of 
Indian Standards prescribe the safety norms, the design norms, the structural 
norms and the soil testing norms for each category of the vulnerable zone. That 
is already in place. 
Unfortunately, they were not there in  the building codes of some of the 
State Governments. We had written to them about a year-and-a-half ago saying 
that such and such is your vulnerability and such an such are the building 
codes to be followed. We requested them to kindly incorporate those codes in 
their bye-laws so that they could be statutorily enforced. Unfortunately, the 
State Governments did not do them. But, after the recent earthquake, we have 
again written to them, and I have personally written to the Chief Ministers 
twice. In the case of Delhi, we have taken initiatives and issued notifications 
also inviting public reaction, because th at is the requirement of the law. So, 
these measure will ensure that. 
Now, the National Building code of the Bureau of Indian Standards must 
be followed by all concerned. So far as the Government departments are 
concerned, they are following it on their own. For example, the Central Public 
Works Department is following the norms of the Bureau of Indian Standards. 
The DDA is following thai. All the Government departments are following. 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [26th February, 2001] 
I would like to inform this House that about 500 CPWD buildings were in that 
zone, which were affected by the eart hquake in Gujarat, whether Bhuj or 
Ahmedabad. Only three buildings have been damaged to the extent of collapse, out 
of the more than 500 buildings. This is because we are following these codes. 
Of course, in zone-3, because people were cutting comers and creating all types of 
problems they were not followed. In the case of flyovers and irrigation projects, these 
standards are required to be followed and they are given in the codes. We are again 
asking them to follow those standards. 
I have invited all the Ministers concerned for a meeting on the 14th, March. 
I am again going to request them to ensure that these standards prescribed by the 
Bureau are incorported in the bye-laws and they are followed scrupulously. Another 
point which I would like to inform this House arising out of this is that this will apply 
to the buildings which have yet to come up. There are building which have already 
been constructed or irrigations projects which have already been completed. So, 
there also we have published technical guidelines on how to retrofit those 
buildings how to improve the strength of those buildings and how to ensure that 
they do not get damaged. Even with regard to buildings which have been 
damaged, we have defined the degree of the damage. Something which has to be 
rebuilt is G-5; then there is G-4 which can be reconstructed with slight changes and 
then G-3 which can be done with a little more effort. Then there are G-l with 
superficial cracks which can be easily repaired. We have defined all these things so 
that no unnessary expenditure takes place in demolishing building which can be 
retrofitted, and they should be retrofitted. So, our code, what 1 call the techno-legal 
regime, which we are formulating will ta ke care of these eventualities. This 
techno-legal regime is being promoted by us. We are requesting the State 
Governments that all building agencies should adopt them and also incorporate them 
in their bye-laws so that anyone deviating from these laws is made answerable to the 
public authorities.

The fees payable to the advisors generally consist of two components.

gross proceeds to be received by the Government from the disinvestments.

from disinvestments, quantum of work required to complete the transaction, 
degree of difficulty and chances of suc cess of the transaction etc. Further, 
Consultants appointed for disinvestments through joint venture route are given 
flat/fixed/lumpsum fee/asset valuation fee/out of pocket expenditure depending
